ratings.rationale: Compromised association changes track identity and measurement membership, potentially producing displaced or fabricated tracks or suppressing genuine tracks. No mechanism is cited. L3 consistency checks may detect anomalies, but W2 and W3 concern measurement bias, not arbitrary association corruption.
ratings.issue: The record omits downstream integrity-monitor and cross-check effects; association errors may be detected differently from numerical measurement biases.

ratings.rationale: Altering the detection predicates can suppress genuine discrepancy indications or create false alarms across the surveillance service. It directly compromises integrity verdicts, rather than merely biasing measurements. No published mechanism supports reproducibility.
ratings.issue: The named asset A3.4 is incomplete: the mechanism explicitly includes A3.5. Detection of compromised logic requires independent monitoring outside the affected modules.

ratings.rationale: Corrupt ephemeris or clock-state inputs bias localisation across multiple measurements. This is data tampering, not necessarily temporal integrity: the authentication-invariance test distinguishes stored-state corruption from an actual time-reference offset. W2 and W3 govern detectability of equivalent biases.
ratings.issue: The equivalence to clock bias is underspecified; ephemeris corruption and clock-state corruption have different observability and detection properties.

ratings.rationale: Modification of associated solver inputs directly corrupts existing observables. Transport authentication cannot protect against modification after receipt. The resulting measurement bias can cause displacement or denial, with detectability depending on the STRONG or WEAK pass.
ratings.issue: The record overlaps T3.03 in its resulting numerical bias but differs in the corrupted object; clarify whether it includes arbitrary observable fields or only timing values.

ratings.rationale: Resource exhaustion can prevent timely localisation and tracking, degrading surveillance availability. The cited conference material is not independently assessable here and does not establish an ADS-B LEO-specific demonstration. Platform or service monitoring may reveal degradation.
ratings.issue: The cited source concerns spacecraft vulnerabilities, not necessarily solver exhaustion. The record conflates input flooding, computational complexity and track-database exhaustion.

ratings.rationale: Threshold relaxation widens the conditions under which biased solutions escape detection. It is an enabler because it changes the effectiveness of other threats rather than independently creating a corrupted target report. Governance configuration is also implicated.
ratings.issue: The mechanism is an enabler, not an independent displacement event. The configuration-management asset A4.4 is omitted from the authors' asset list.

ratings.rationale: Consistent fabrication of broadcast and independent surveillance positions defeats the intended independence of the cross-check, producing a falsely verified target. Multi-device multilateration spoofing supports the general mechanism, but not necessarily the complete LEO implementation.
ratings.issue: The record assumes coordinated corruption of both independent positions without adequately establishing feasibility or distinguishing genuine aircraft deception from fabricated-target injection.

ratings.rationale: Perturbing one position creates a false discrepancy and causes a genuine aircraft to be marked suspect. The principal effect is integrity-verdict deception, potentially denying confidence in a real target. Detection is the intended function of the cross-check.
ratings.issue: The affected asset depends on which position is perturbed. A discrepancy alone does not establish that an ATM controller receives an incorrect operational verdict.

ratings.rationale: Output modification occurs after the L3 detection predicates, allowing altered reports or integrity annotations to reach ATM without those checks evaluating the final product. It is downstream data tampering, distinct from solver-input corruption.
ratings.issue: The threat should distinguish content alteration, integrity-annotation alteration and report suppression; these have different consequences and detection opportunities.

ratings.rationale: Unauthorised reading of stored tracks and reports exposes non-public aircraft movements. It has a disclosure-only consequence under the specified goals and does not itself enable another catalogue threat.
ratings.issue: A3.6 is an encoder, not the track database. The record should identify actual storage, logs, access controls and the sensitivity of disclosed traffic.

ratings.rationale: Altering audit trails undermines attribution and forensic reconstruction. This is primarily repudiation, not a direct change to surveillance output. It is an enabler for other compromises, especially broad platform compromise.
ratings.issue: Not a strict duplicate of platform compromise, but its dependence on privileged access and shared hosting makes it an overlapping post-compromise capability rather than a distinct entry threat.

ratings.rationale: Compromise of the common hosting platform grants control over the processing modules, enabling arbitrary changes to measurements, integrity decisions and delivered reports. The cited material is not independently verified and is analogue evidence.
ratings.issue: The record conflates remote exploitation, privilege escalation and full host control. Separate initial access, privilege acquisition and resulting module compromise.

missing_threats.title: Unauthorised measurement-association manipulation through database poisoning
missing_threats.why: Persistent poisoning of association state or reference mappings may evade detection differently from transient association logic exploitation.

missing_threats.title: Track identity and lifecycle corruption
missing_threats.why: Track initiation, continuation, merging and termination errors deserve explicit coverage independently of solver numerical corruption.

missing_threats.title: Integrity-monitor availability failure
missing_threats.why: A failed or unavailable monitor may cause fail-open behaviour or stale integrity annotations without deliberate threshold modification.

missing_threats.title: ASTERIX interface replay and sequencing corruption
missing_threats.why: Replay, stale reports and sequencing inconsistencies can compromise freshness and operational track continuity.

missing_threats.title: Cross-tenant or virtualisation isolation failure
missing_threats.why: Isolation failures may expose or alter processing workloads without requiring full compromise of the central platform.

rubric_ambiguities: W2 and W3 specify single-satellite measurement-bias detection, not detection of association, software, database or integrity-logic compromise.
The rubric does not specify how to score affected users when a common platform compromise can affect the entire constellation but only selected reports.
The evidence rubric does not clearly distinguish a general vulnerability demonstration from evidence of the specific mechanism claimed.
The analogue-only deduction is defined, but evidence levels for non-peer-reviewed conference talks are not explicitly calibrated.
The temporal-integrity authentication-invariance test does not clearly address corruption of stored clock-state estimates rather than physical time references.
batch_comments.overall: The batch covers important L3 integrity, availability, confidentiality and platform risks. Its main weakness is inconsistent separation of root compromise, specific data manipulation and downstream consequences. Several records lack supporting evidence, and W2/W3 should not be mechanically applied to software and association attacks. The cross-check threats require especially careful separation of fabricated targets from false alarms against genuine aircraft.
